claim: Neural tube closure defects are a major cause of infant mortality, with exencephaly accounting for nearly one-third of cases.
source: Neural tube closure defects are a major cause of infant mortality, with exencephaly accounting for nearly one-third of cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on neural tube defects.

claim: Midline cells in the mouse midbrain neuroepithelium are flat with large apical surfaces during neural tube closure.
source: Midline cells in the mouse midbrain neuroepithelium are flat with large apical surfaces, whereas lateral cells are taller and undergo synchronous apical constriction, driving neural fold elevation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing cell morphology measurements.

claim: Lateral cells in the mouse midbrain neuroepithelium are taller and undergo synchronous apical constriction during neural fold elevation.
source: Midline cells in the mouse midbrain neuroepithelium are flat with large apical surfaces, whereas lateral cells are taller and undergo synchronous apical constriction, driving neural fold elevation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing cell height and apical area measurements in lateral cells.

claim: Embryos lacking the Shh effector Gli2 fail to produce appropriate midline cell architecture.
source: Embryos lacking the Shh effector Gli2 fail to produce appropriate midline cell architecture, whereas embryos with expanded Shh signaling, including the IFT-A complex mutants Ift122 and Ttc21b and embryos expressing activated Smoothened, display apical constriction defects in lateral cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Gli2 mutant analysis showing altered midline cell morphology.

claim: IFT-A complex mutants Ift122 and Ttc21b display apical constriction defects in lateral cells.
source: Embryos lacking the Shh effector Gli2 fail to produce appropriate midline cell architecture, whereas embryos with expanded Shh signaling, including the IFT-A complex mutants Ift122 and Ttc21b and embryos expressing activated Smoothened, display apical constriction defects in lateral cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased apical cell area in lateral cells of Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants.

claim: Embryos expressing activated Smoothened display apical constriction defects in lateral cells.
source: Embryos lacking the Shh effector Gli2 fail to produce appropriate midline cell architecture, whereas embryos with expanded Shh signaling, including the IFT-A complex mutants Ift122 and Ttc21b and embryos expressing activated Smoothened, display apical constriction defects in lateral cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SmoM2-expressing embryos showing increased apical area in lateral cells.

claim: Disruption of lateral, but not midline, cell remodeling results in exencephaly.
source: Disruption of lateral, but not midline, cell remodeling results in exencephaly.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that Gli2 mutants with midline defects close normally, while IFT-A mutants and SmoM2-expressing embryos with lateral cell defects develop exencephaly.

claim: Neural tube closure defects occur in 1 in 1000 pregnancies worldwide.
source: Neural tube closure defects are among the most common structural birth defects, occurring in 1 in 1000 pregnancies worldwide (Wallingford et al., 2013; Zaganjor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: One-third of human neural tube defects arise from a failure of closure in the cranial region, resulting in exencephaly.
source: Although many studies have focused on mechanisms of neural tube closure in the spinal cord, one-third of human neural tube defects arise from a failure of closure in the cranial region, resulting in exencephaly—an inoperable and terminally lethal birth defect (Zaganjor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to epidemiological literature.

claim: Exencephaly is an inoperable and terminally lethal birth defect.
source: Although many studies have focused on mechanisms of neural tube closure in the spinal cord, one-third of human neural tube defects arise from a failure of closure in the cranial region, resulting in exencephaly—an inoperable and terminally lethal birth defect (Zaganjor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to clinical literature and represents established medical knowledge.

claim: More than a hundred genes are specifically required for closure of the mouse cranial neural plate.
source: More than a hundred genes are specifically required for closure of the mouse cranial neural plate, suggesting that unique mechanisms promote neural tube closure in the cranial region (Harris and Juriloff, 2007; Harris and Juriloff, 2010; Wilde et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genetic studies in mice.

claim: The neural plate is significantly wider in the cranial region compared with the spinal cord.
source: The neural plate is significantly wider in the cranial region compared with the spinal cord, suggesting that distinct strategies are required for closure of the developing brain.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge and inference about functional implications.

claim: High levels of Shh produce ventral cell fates in the neural tube.
source: Neuronal identities at different mediolateral positions are regulated by the secreted Shh, Wnt, and BMP proteins, with high levels of Shh producing ventral cell fates, moderate levels of Shh producing intermediate cell fates, and high levels of Wnt and BMP producing dorsal cell fates (McMahon et al., 2003; Dessaud et al., 2008; Sagner and Briscoe, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on Shh signaling and cell fate specification.

claim: Moderate levels of Shh produce intermediate cell fates in the neural tube.
source: Neuronal identities at different mediolateral positions are regulated by the secreted Shh, Wnt, and BMP proteins, with high levels of Shh producing ventral cell fates, moderate levels of Shh producing intermediate cell fates, and high levels of Wnt and BMP producing dorsal cell fates (McMahon et al., 2003; Dessaud et al., 2008; Sagner and Briscoe, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on Shh signaling.

claim: High levels of Wnt and BMP produce dorsal cell fates in the neural tube.
source: Neuronal identities at different mediolateral positions are regulated by the secreted Shh, Wnt, and BMP proteins, with high levels of Shh producing ventral cell fates, moderate levels of Shh producing intermediate cell fates, and high levels of Wnt and BMP producing dorsal cell fates (McMahon et al., 2003; Dessaud et al., 2008; Sagner and Briscoe, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on neural patterning.

claim: Spatially restricted Shh and BMP signaling are required for local tissue bending in the posterior spinal cord.
source: In the posterior spinal cord, spatially restricted Shh and BMP signaling are required for local tissue bending, suggesting that these signals can influence tissue structure as well as cell identity (Ybot-Gonzalez et al., 2002; Ybot-Gonzalez et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on spinal cord morphogenesis.

claim: Lateral cells displayed a more than 50% decrease in apical area between 0 and 9 somites.
source: Lateral cells on either side of the midline displayed a more than 50% decrease in apical area between 0 and 9 somites (Figure 1F–H, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of apical cell area shown in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The average apical surface area of midline cells did not change significantly during elevation.
source: By contrast, the average apical surface area of midline cells did not change significantly during elevation (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Lateral cells became progressively mediolaterally oriented during elevation.
source: Additionally, lateral cells became progressively mediolaterally oriented during the same period, whereas midline cell orientation was unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell orientation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Midline cell orientation was unchanged during elevation.
source: Additionally, lateral cells became progressively mediolaterally oriented during the same period, whereas midline cell orientation was unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell orientation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell height in the lateral and midline regions did not change significantly during early elevation (0–7 somites).
source: Cell height in the lateral and midline regions did not change significantly during early elevation (0–7 somites) (Figure 3C and D), even though the average apical area of lateral cells decreased by more than 30% during this period (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell height measurements shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Lateral and midline cells elongated more than 60% along the apical-basal axis after the 7-somite stage.
source: By contrast, lateral and midline cells elongated more than 60% along the apical-basal axis after the 7-somite stage, such that lateral cells were consistently taller than midline cells throughout elevation (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell height measurements shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Lateral cells were consistently taller than midline cells throughout elevation.
source: By contrast, lateral and midline cells elongated more than 60% along the apical-basal axis after the 7-somite stage, such that lateral cells were consistently taller than midline cells throughout elevation (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell height measurements and ratios shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Cell remodeling in the elevating midbrain occurs in two phases: an early phase involving apical remodeling without changes in cell height, and a later phase involving apicobasal elongation.
source: Thus, cell remodeling in the elevating midbrain occurs in two phases, with an early phase involving apical remodeling in the absence of changes in cell height, and a later phase involving apicobasal elongation (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal analysis of cell height and apical area changes shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The conversion of the midbrain neural plate from convex to concave is accompanied by a decrease in the apical span of the tissue without a significant change in the basal span.
source: Consistent with this possibility, the conversion of the midbrain neural plate from convex to concave is accompanied by a decrease in the apical span of the tissue without a significant change in the basal span (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements of apical and basal spans shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: More than half of lateral cells (51 ± 6%) had a highly constricted apical neck.
source: More than half of lateral cells (51 ± 6%) had a highly constricted apical neck, a hallmark of apical constriction.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of individual cell morphologies using mosaic membrane-GFP labeling.

claim: An additional 13 ± 2% of lateral cells displayed properties consistent with apical constriction, but with a shorter neck domain.
source: An additional 13 ± 2% of cells displayed properties consistent with apical constriction, but with a shorter neck domain, suggesting that apical area changes can occur even in the absence of a basal shift in cell volume.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis of lateral cells shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Midline cells tended to be columnar (45 ± 5%) or apically expanded (30%).
source: In contrast to lateral cells, midline cells tended to be columnar (45 ± 5%) or apically expanded (30%), with relatively few midline cells showing apically constricted morphologies (17 ± 3%) (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by manual segmentation and analysis of midline cell shapes shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Relatively few midline cells showed apically constricted morphologies (17 ± 3%).
source: In contrast to lateral cells, midline cells tended to be columnar (45 ± 5%) or apically expanded (30%), with relatively few midline cells showing apically constricted morphologies (17 ± 3%) (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of midline cell morphologies.

claim: The Ift122TR2 mutation is a single C to A mutation at position 115,899,529 on chromosome 6, resulting in a premature stop codon that truncates the protein at amino acid 575 (out of 1138).
source: The Ift122TR2 mutation was mapped to a single C to A mutation at position 115,899,529 on chromosome 6, resulting in a premature stop codon that is predicted to truncate the protein at amino acid 575 (out of 1138).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic mapping data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Ttc21bTF2 allele is a single C to A mutation at position 66,242,780 on chromosome 2, resulting in a premature stop codon that truncates the protein at amino acid position 187 (out of 1,315).
source: The Ttc21bTF2 allele was mapped to a single C to A mutation at position 66,242,780 on chromosome 2, resulting in a premature stop codon that is predicted to truncate the protein at amino acid position 187 (out of 1,315).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic mapping data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ift122 and Ttc21b mutant embryos exhibited a reduction in the number of cilia.
source: Consistent with these functions, mutant embryos from both strains exhibited a reduction in the number of cilia (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis of cilia markers shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants failed to generate V-shaped neural folds in the midbrain, forebrain, and anterior hindbrain regions of 7-somite embryos.
source: In contrast to littermate controls, which completed neural fold elevation, apposition, and fusion in 24 hr, Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants failed to generate V-shaped neural folds in the midbrain, forebrain, and anterior hindbrain regions of 7-somite embryos (Figure 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 4 and associated supplements.

claim: The cranial neural folds of Ift122 and Ttc21b mutant embryos remained unelevated at all stages analyzed, leading to highly penetrant exencephaly at E10.5.
source: These defects did not recover and the cranial neural folds of mutant embryos remained unelevated at all stages analyzed, leading to highly penetrant exencephaly at E10.5 (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal analysis of mutant embryos shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Exencephaly was observed in 10/10 Ift122 mutants compared with 0/16 WT controls.
source: Exencephaly was observed in 10/10 Ift122 mutants (B) (compared with 0/16 WT controls) and 5/5 Ttc21b mutants (C) (compared with 0/13 WT controls).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of exencephaly penetrance shown in Figure 4.

claim: Exencephaly was observed in 5/5 Ttc21b mutants compared with 0/13 WT controls.
source: Exencephaly was observed in 10/10 Ift122 mutants (B) (compared with 0/16 WT controls) and 5/5 Ttc21b mutants (C) (compared with 0/13 WT controls).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of exencephaly penetrance shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lateral cells in Ift122 mutants displayed a 55% increase in average apical cell area compared with littermate controls.
source: Lateral cells in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants displayed a 55% and 93% increase in average apical cell area, respectively, compared with littermate controls (Figure 4J–M), as well as altered cell orientation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of apical cell area shown in Figure 4J-M.

claim: Lateral cells in Ttc21b mutants displayed a 93% increase in average apical cell area compared with littermate controls.
source: Lateral cells in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants displayed a 55% and 93% increase in average apical cell area, respectively, compared with littermate controls (Figure 4J–M), as well as altered cell orientation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of apical cell area shown in Figure 4J-M.

claim: Ift122 and Ttc21b mutant embryos had a normal frequency and distribution of mitotic cells along the mediolateral axis.
source: These defects did not result from reduced cell proliferation, as mutant embryos had a normal frequency and distribution of mitotic cells along the mediolateral axis, and normal cell density in the underlying mesenchyme (Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by phospho-histone H3 staining analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Ift122 and Ttc21b mutant embryos had normal cell density in the underlying mesenchyme.
source: These defects did not result from reduced cell proliferation, as mutant embryos had a normal frequency and distribution of mitotic cells along the mediolateral axis, and normal cell density in the underlying mesenchyme (Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by DAPI staining analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: In wild-type controls, apically expanded cells were present at the midline and at the outer margins of the tissue, separated by a broad domain of apically constricted cells spanning 30–40 cell diameters along the mediolateral axis and more than 60 cells along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: In wild-type littermate controls, apically expanded cells were present at the midline and at the outer margins of the tissue. These domains were separated by a broad domain of apically constricted cells spanning 30–40 cell diameters along the mediolateral axis and more than 60 cells along the anterior-posterior axis, encompassing a region of more than 2000 lateral cells on either side of the midline (Figure 5A and F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of cell shapes shown in Figure 5.

claim: The broad domain of apically constricted cells encompasses a region of more than 2000 lateral cells on either side of the midline.
source: In wild-type littermate controls, apically expanded cells were present at the midline and at the outer margins of the tissue. These domains were separated by a broad domain of apically constricted cells spanning 30–40 cell diameters along the mediolateral axis and more than 60 cells along the anterior-posterior axis, encompassing a region of more than 2000 lateral cells on either side of the midline (Figure 5A and F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the spatial extent of apical constriction.

claim: The difference between midline and lateral cell populations was eliminated in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants.
source: The difference between midline and lateral populations was eliminated in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of cell shapes across the mediolateral axis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants, lateral cells were apically expanded and midline cells were apically constricted compared with controls.
source: In mutant embryos, lateral cells were apically expanded and midline cells were apically constricted compared with controls, whereas cell shape at the outer margins of the neural plate was independent of IFT-A activity (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of cell shapes shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: Cell shape at the outer margins of the neural plate was independent of IFT-A activity.
source: In mutant embryos, lateral cells were apically expanded and midline cells were apically constricted compared with controls, whereas cell shape at the outer margins of the neural plate was independent of IFT-A activity (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis showing no difference in cell shape at the margins in mutants versus controls.

claim: The difference in height between wild-type midline and lateral cells was abolished in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants.
source: Moreover, the difference in height between wild-type midline and lateral cells was abolished in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants (Figure 5I and J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell height measurements shown in Figure 5I-J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Actomyosin cables in wild-type embryos were present at a range of orientations, with a strong mediolateral bias.
source: In line with these observations, we observed frequent supracellular cables in the elevating cranial neural plate. Cables were present at a range of orientations, with a strong mediolateral bias (Figure 6A,B,E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of cable orientation shown in Figure 6.

claim: Fewer actomyosin cables were present in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants, and the cables that did form were not consistently oriented with respect to the mediolateral axis.
source: By contrast, fewer actomyosin cables were present in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants, and the cables that did form were not consistently oriented with respect to the mediolateral axis (Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cable number and orientation shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ratio of phosphomyosin to F-actin at adherens junctions was decreased in Ttc21b mutants.
source: The ratio of phosphomyosin to F-actin at adherens junctions was also decreased in Ttc21b mutants (Figure 6G and H), consistent with the stronger apical constriction defects in this mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of phosphomyosin and F-actin intensity shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: In wild-type embryos, Nkx6.1 levels were highest at the midline during midbrain neural fold elevation and decreased with increasing distance from the midline.
source: In wild-type embryos, Nkx6.1 levels were highest at the midline during midbrain neural fold elevation and decreased with increasing distance from the midline (Figure 7A and B), consistent with results at later stages (Qiu et al., 1998; Tran et al., 2008; Qin et al., 2011; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nkx6.1 immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Nkx6.1 was expressed at lower levels in the anterior hindbrain, revealing differential regulation along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: In addition, Nkx6.1 was expressed at lower levels in the anterior hindbrain, revealing differential regulation along the anterior-posterior axis (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nkx6.1 expression analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants, the mediolateral pattern of Nkx6.1 expression was abolished, and Nkx6.1 was expressed at equivalent, intermediate levels in midline and lateral cells.
source: In Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants, the mediolateral pattern of Nkx6.1 expression was abolished, and Nkx6.1 was expressed at equivalent, intermediate levels in midline and lateral cells (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nkx6.1 expression analysis in mutants shown in Figure 7.

claim: In Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants, the mediolateral extent of the Nkx6.1 domain was expanded, reaching all the way to the neural plate borders.
source: In addition, the mediolateral extent of the Nkx6.1 domain was expanded, reaching all the way to the neural plate borders in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of Nkx6.1 expression in mutants.

claim: The anterior-posterior pattern of Nkx6.1 expression was unaffected in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants, indicating that this axis of Shh regulation is independent of IFT-A activity.
source: By contrast, the anterior-posterior pattern of Nkx6.1 expression was unaffected, indicating that this axis of Shh regulation is independent of IFT-A activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of Nkx6.1 expression patterns along the anterior-posterior axis in mutants versus controls.

claim: Gli2 mutants failed to establish ventral cell fates in the elevating midbrain, including FoxA2 expression in the floor plate.
source: Consistent with the effects of Gli2 at later stages, Gli2 mutants failed to establish ventral cell fates in the elevating midbrain, including FoxA2 expression in the floor plate, indicating that Gli2 is required for midline cell identity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by FoxA2 and Nkx6.1 expression analysis in Gli2 mutants shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Midline cells in Gli2 mutants had a significant decrease in apical area compared with wild type.
source: Midline cells in Gli2 mutants had a significant decrease in apical area compared with wild type (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of midline cell apical area shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: Midline cells in Gli2 mutants were significantly taller than in wild-type controls.
source: In addition, midline cells in Gli2 mutants were significantly taller than in wild-type controls (Figure 8G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell height measurements shown in Figure 8G-H.

claim: Lateral cell morphology was unaffected in Gli2 mutants.
source: By contrast, lateral cell morphology was unaffected in Gli2 mutants (Figure 8A–C,G and H), and no defects in cell orientation were observed in either region (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lateral cell apical area and height in Gli2 mutants shown in Figure 8.

claim: No defects in cell orientation were observed in either lateral or midline regions in Gli2 mutants.
source: By contrast, lateral cell morphology was unaffected in Gli2 mutants (Figure 8A–C,G and H), and no defects in cell orientation were observed in either region (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell orientation analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gli2 mutants complete closure normally in both cranial and spinal regions.
source: Despite these severe midline defects, Gli2 mutants complete closure normally in both cranial and spinal regions (Mo et al., 1997; Matise et al., 1998; Bai and Joyner, 2001), indicating that the specialized architecture of midline cells is dispensable for cranial neural tube closure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Gli2 mutant phenotypes.

claim: The specialized architecture of midline cells is dispensable for cranial neural tube closure.
source: Despite these severe midline defects, Gli2 mutants complete closure normally in both cranial and spinal regions (Mo et al., 1997; Matise et al., 1998; Bai and Joyner, 2001), indicating that the specialized architecture of midline cells is dispensable for cranial neural tube closure.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Gli2 mutants with altered midline cell morphology still complete neural tube closure normally.

claim: SmoM2-expressing embryos have expanded Nkx6.1 expression throughout the midbrain.
source: SmoM2-expressing embryos have expanded Nkx6.1 expression throughout the midbrain, consistent with uniform activation of the Shh response (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Nkx6.1 expression analysis in SmoM2-expressing embryos shown in Figure 9C-D.

claim: SmoM2 expression did not affect cell proliferation or cell orientation.
source: SmoM2 expression did not affect cell proliferation or cell orientation (Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of proliferation and cell orientation shown in Figure 9—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: SmoM2 expression resulted in a 50% increase in apical area in lateral cells.
source: However, SmoM2 expression resulted in a 50% increase in apical area in lateral cells (Figure 9G–I), similar to the defects in Ift122 mutants, but less severe than the defects in Ttc21b mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of lateral cell apical area in SmoM2-expressing embryos shown in Figure 9G-I.

claim: Cells that did not express Wnt1-Cre2 apically constricted normally, suggesting that activated SmoM2 acts cell autonomously to regulate cell shape.
source: The effects of SmoM2 were localized, as cells that did not express Wnt1-Cre2 apically constricted normally, suggesting that activated SmoM2 acts cell autonomously to regulate cell shape (Figure 9E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mosaic analysis of SmoM2-expressing and non-expressing cells shown in Figure 9E-F.

claim: SmoM2-expressing embryos did not display morphological defects at the midline.
source: SmoM2-expressing embryos did not display morphological defects at the midline, perhaps because Smoothened activation did not further enhance the already high Shh response in this region (Figure 9G,J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of midline cell morphology in SmoM2-expressing embryos shown in Figure 9G, J-K.

claim: SmoM2-expressing embryos exhibited 100% penetrant exencephaly (12/12 SmoM2-expressing embryos compared with 0/13 littermate controls).
source: Notably, SmoM2-expressing embryos exhibited 100% penetrant exencephaly (12/12 SmoM2-expressing embryos compared with 0/13 littermate controls) (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of exencephaly penetrance shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Disruption of apical constriction in lateral cells alone—in the absence of structural changes at the midline—is sufficient to prevent cranial neural closure.
source: These results demonstrate that disruption of apical constriction in lateral cells alone—in the absence of structural changes at the midline—is sufficient to prevent cranial neural closure.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that SmoM2-expressing embryos with lateral cell defects but normal midline morphology develop exencephaly.

claim: Patterned Shh signaling in the midbrain neuroepithelium is required for spatially regulated apical remodeling events that drive cranial neural closure.
source: Thus, patterned Shh signaling in the midbrain neuroepithelium is required for spatially regulated apical remodeling events that drive cranial neural closure, and dysregulation of Shh activity leads to altered cell remodeling and exencephaly (Figure 9L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data from Gli2, IFT-A, and SmoM2 experiments showing that disruption of Shh patterning leads to altered cell morphology and exencephaly.

claim: Dysregulation of Shh activity leads to altered cell remodeling and exencephaly.
source: Thus, patterned Shh signaling in the midbrain neuroepithelium is required for spatially regulated apical remodeling events that drive cranial neural closure, and dysregulation of Shh activity leads to altered cell remodeling and exencephaly (Figure 9L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from multiple mutants showing that altered Shh signaling correlates with cell remodeling defects and exencephaly.

claim: Elevation of the cranial neural folds is driven by the synchronous, sustained apical constriction of a large population of lateral cells.
source: In contrast to the spinal cord, elevation of the cranial neural folds is driven by the synchronous, sustained apical constriction of a large population of lateral cells, whereas midline cells remain flat and apically expanded.
evidence: This claim is supported by temporal and spatial analysis of cell morphology during neural fold elevation.

claim: Loss of the IFT-A complex components Ift122 or Ttc21b disrupt apical constriction and actomyosin organization in lateral cells, resulting in a failure of cranial neural tube closure.
source: The loss of Gli2, a transcriptional effector of Shh signaling, disrupts cell architecture at the midline, whereas loss of the IFT-A complex components Ift122 or Ttc21b disrupt apical constriction and actomyosin organization in lateral cells, resulting in a failure of cranial neural tube closure.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing increased apical area, disrupted actomyosin organization, and exencephaly in Ift122 and Ttc21b mutants.

claim: Lateral cells drive cranial neural tube closure through large-scale, coordinated apical constriction behaviors that are spatially regulated by patterned Shh activity.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that lateral cells drive cranial neural tube closure through large-scale, coordinated apical constriction behaviors that are spatially regulated by patterned Shh activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined data showing that lateral cell apical constriction is essential for closure and is regulated by Shh signaling.

claim: Apical constriction is a highly conserved process that transforms columnar epithelial cells into wedge shapes through actomyosin-dependent contraction of the apical cell surface.
source: Apical constriction is a highly conserved process that transforms columnar epithelial cells into wedge shapes through actomyosin-dependent contraction of the apical cell surface and drives structural changes such as cell ingression, tissue bending, and tissue invagination (Martin and Goldstein, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review on apical constriction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the amphibian neural plate, apical constriction is required to form the median and dorsolateral hinge points.
source: In the amphibian neural plate, apical constriction is required to form the median and dorsolateral hinge points, two localized tissue bending events that are a prerequisite for closure (Burnside and Jacobson, 1968; Burnside, 1973; Haigo et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2007; Itoh et al., 2014; Ossipova et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on amphibian neural tube closure.

claim: In the mouse spinal cord, neural tube closure is independent of actomyosin activity.
source: In the mouse spinal cord, neural tube closure is independent of actomyosin activity, suggesting that apical constriction is not required for this process (Ybot-Gonzalez and Copp, 1999; Escuin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on mouse spinal cord closure.

claim: Regulators of actin and myosin are required for closure of the cranial neural plate.
source: By contrast, regulators of actin and myosin are required for closure of the cranial neural plate, although the cell behaviors that are controlled by this contractile machinery are unclear (Morriss-Kay and Tuckett, 1985; Hildebrand and Soriano, 1999; Brouns et al., 2000; McGreevy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on actomyosin function in cranial neural tube closure.
